title: PSLOG: Pretraining with Search Logs for Document Ranking

problem.claim: The work addresses pretraining ranking models for information retrieval using search-log supervision.

gap.claim: Existing methods mainly use direct query-document click signals, leaving other supervision signals in search logs underexplored.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes leveraging four query-document relevance relations, including co-interaction and multi-hop relations, for IR pretraining.
The method constructs an Interaction Graph from all search logs to represent global query-document relevance relations.
The method proposes four strategies for generating contrastive positive and negative query-document pairs for ranking-model pretraining.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments on industrial and academic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.

narrative_sequence.summary: Pretrained models perform strongly in NLP and IR, and IR-oriented pretraining can outperform only fine-tuning pretrained language models on IR datasets.
Search logs provide implicit relevance judgments under concrete queries.
Existing methods focus mainly on direct click signals, while other search-log supervision remains insufficiently explored.
The proposed method models global query-document relations with an Interaction Graph and uses four relation-based strategies to generate contrastive pretraining pairs.
Experiments are reported on industrial and academic datasets.

source_observation.claim: Search logs contain implicit relevance judgments and relations beyond direct query-document clicks.

interpretation.claim: Behavioral logs may support richer supervision when represented through relational structure.

application.claim: For ranking pretraining, consider graph-derived co-interaction and multi-hop relations in addition to direct clicks.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which relation types or pair-generation strategies are most effective.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the four relevance relations individually.
The abstract does not report quantitative results, baselines, dataset names, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not describe the ranking models or pretraining implementation details.
